note: The circle of the lustful, and the first where sins are actively punished. Circles two to five hold the sins of weak self-control: lust, gluttony, greed and anger. They are the least grave, so they lie highest.
Hell is a funnel. Each circle down is a narrower ring, with worse pain.

context: In the Aeneid he is a solemn judge who questions the dead. Dante keeps his office but makes him a snarling demon with a tail.

note: The number of coils is the sentence: two for the second circle, nine for the bottom of Hell.
A grim copy of the Church's confession. The souls tell everything, unable to hold anything back, but too late: no forgiveness follows, only the sentence.
An echo of the Gospel: "wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leads to destruction" (Matthew 7:13). Getting into Hell is easy.

quote: This is willed where power exists
note: The same formula that silenced Charon in Canto 3: the journey is willed in Heaven, where whatever is willed can be done.
The punishment mirrors the sin. In life these souls let passion carry them wherever it blew. Now a wind does the same, in the dark, forever.

Dante's word is simply "the ruin", and its meaning is debated. Many commentators take it for a landslide left by the earthquake at Christ's death, which Virgil describes in Inferno 12. The sight of it would remind the souls of the salvation they lost, which is why they curse God here.

quote: who made reason slave to desire
note: Dante's definition of lust, and of all the sins of the upper circles. Desire is not evil in itself. The sin is letting it rule the reason that should rule it.
The first of three bird similes in the canto. The mass of the lustful are starlings, tossed about in a flock. Those who died for love are cranes in a long line. The two lovers will come like doves.

context: Dante follows the Christian historian Orosius, who says she made incest lawful to cover her own with her son. The Italian packs the decree into a famous play on words: she made libito (pleasure) licito (lawful).

note: The legendary king of Assyria and founder of Nineveh. Semiramis was his widow and ruled after him.

quote: the land the Sultan now controls
note: In 1300 the Sultan ruled Egypt and Syria, not Semiramis's Mesopotamia. Dante may be confusing her Babylon with the Egyptian fortress town of the same name, near modern Cairo, a common mix-up in his time.

quote: she who killed herself for love
context: Not named until line 80. Sichaeus was her murdered husband, and she had vowed to stay faithful to his memory. Dante puts her here for her love, not lower down among the suicides.
The "ruthless years" are the ten years of the Trojan War, fought to win her back.

Dante didn't know Homer's Iliad, only the medieval retellings of Troy. In those, Achilles falls in love with the Trojan princess Polyxena and is lured unarmed to a temple, where Paris kills him. Love was his last fight.
The only modern name in the list. With him the roll call moves from ancient history to the love stories Dante's own generation read.

note: Dante sees the heroes of Greece and Troy as figures from a medieval romance, ladies and knights. It prepares the meeting to come, with two lovers undone by reading one.

context: Francesca and her lover Paolo, her husband's brother. Every other soul here is blown about alone. She is not named until line 111, and he is never named at all.

note: The line of souls Virgil has just pointed out, those who died because of love. Francesca and Paolo, killed for theirs, belong with them.
Dante's word is perso, which he describes in another work as a mix of purple and black in which the black wins: a color close to darkness.
With their own blood. The two were murdered.

quote: if the King of the universe were our friend
note: Francesca speaks with the manners of a court, and offers a prayer she knows is worth nothing. The damned can't pray, and she doesn't name God.

quote: The city where I was born
note: Ravenna, near the Adriatic coast where the Po reaches the sea. Francesca's family, the da Polenta, were its lords. Dante spent his last years there as the guest of her nephew, Guido Novello da Polenta, and died there in 1321.

quote: Love, which quickly seizes any gentle heart
note: Three sentences in a row begin with "Love". Francesca talks in the language of the love poetry of Dante's youth: the line echoes a famous poem by Guido Guinizzelli, and a sonnet of Dante's own, on love and the noble heart. In her telling Love did everything, and she did nothing.
Usually taken to mean the manner of her death: killed suddenly, in the act, with no time to repent. Some read it instead as the force of Paolo's love, which still overwhelms her.

quote: Love, which allows no beloved not to love in return
note: One of the most famous lines in Italian: Amor, ch'a nullo amato amar perdona. That love must be answered with love was a rule of the courtly love tradition. As an excuse it is false: the will stays free, which is why she is here.

context: Her husband, Gianciotto Malatesta, who killed his wife and his brother. He was still alive in 1300, when the poem is set, so Hell is only waiting for him.

note: Among the best-known lines in the poem. The thought comes from Boethius, who wrote in his Consolation of Philosophy that the unhappiest kind of misfortune is to have been happy.
Probably Virgil, who must remember his life on earth from Limbo. Some early commentators thought she meant Boethius, the source of the saying.

context: They were reading the Old French prose romance of Lancelot, a favorite of the Italian courts.

note: Queen Guinevere's mouth. In the romance it is the queen who kisses Lancelot. Francesca remembers it the other way round, with the man making the first move.

Gallehault, the knight who in the romance brings Lancelot and Guinevere together and urges the kiss. The book and its author did the same for these two. His name became the Italian word for a go-between, and Boccaccio later gave the Decameron the subtitle "Prince Galeotto".

quote: That day we read no further
note: A famous silence: she leaves the rest unsaid. Some readers hear an echo, turned upside down, of Augustine's Confessions, where a book converts him to God and he says he had no wish to read further.
Paolo, who never says a word in the whole canto.

The last line in Italian is famous for its falling sound: E caddi come corpo morto cade. Readers have long argued over Dante's pity. Francesca wins it completely, yet the poet has put her in Hell. Dante had written the kind of love poetry she quotes, so her story accuses him as well.
